key_terms.meaning: The part of a charge's field that varies as 1/r and keeps travelling outward after the charge stops accelerating.
A = μ₀/(4π) ∫ [J]/R dV′, where the current J is evaluated at the earlier time t − R/c so the effect travels at speed c.
A straight current element of length l ≪ λ with uniform current I; its far field is Eθ = jη₀I l sin θ e^(−jβr)/(2λr).
R_r such that ½|I|²R_r equals the power actually radiated; for an infinitesimal dipole R_r = 80π²(l/λ)² Ω.
A plot of radiated field or power against direction (θ, φ), usually normalised to its maximum.
D = 4π U_max / P_rad, the peak radiation intensity divided by the average intensity of the same total power.
G = e_cd · D, directivity reduced by the antenna's radiation efficiency e_cd.
The angular width of the main lobe between the two directions where power falls to half (−3 dB) of the peak.
A_e = λ²D/(4π); the equivalent area from which the antenna captures the incident power density.
The path traced by the tip of the electric field vector in one period: linear, circular or elliptical.
e_cd = P_rad / P_in = R_r/(R_r + R_L); the fraction of accepted power that escapes as radiation, R_L being loss resistance.
R_ff = 2D²/λ, where D is the largest antenna dimension; beyond it the field is locally a plane wave.
Two λ/4 arms fed at the centre, sinusoidal current, R_in ≈ 73 Ω, D = 1.64 (2.15 dBi).
A λ/4 element above an infinite ground plane; it radiates only half the space, so R_in ≈ 36.5 Ω and D = 3.28 (5.15 dBi).
Two parallel half-wave conductors joined at the ends; input resistance is about 4 × 73 = 292 Ω for equal arms.
A loop with circumference ≪ λ carrying near-uniform current; its pattern equals a short dipole's but R_r = 31,171 N²(A/λ²)² Ω is tiny.
An antenna's pattern, impedance and gain are the same whether it transmits or receives; only the feed conditions differ.
P_r = P_t G_t G_r (λ/4πd)², giving the power a matched receiver collects over a free-space path of length d.
The Friis equation written in decibels as a sum of gains and losses, used to check that received power clears the receiver threshold.
Effective isotropic radiated power, EIRP = P_t G_t, the single number that fixes the strength of a transmitter in a link budget.

takeaways: Only an accelerating charge produces the 1/r field that survives as radiation; a charge at constant velocity carries only its near field with it.
The Hertzian dipole gives the sin θ doughnut pattern and shows that field strength falls as 1/r while power density falls as 1/r².
Directivity, gain and beamwidth turn a two-dimensional pattern into three numbers a link budget can multiply.
Radiation resistance converts radiated power into a resistor, so a low R_r compared with loss resistance means poor efficiency.
Effective aperture links a receiving antenna to the incident power density, and A_e = λ²D/4π ties it back to directivity.
All the far-field formulas assume r > 2D²/λ; closer in, the reactive and radiating near fields break the simple rules.
The half-wave dipole is resonant and near 73 Ω, the quarter-wave monopole is its half with half the resistance, and folding adds about 4×.
A small loop radiates like a magnetic dipole, but its radiation resistance is so small that copper loss usually dominates.
Reciprocity lets you measure an antenna in transmit and use the results for receive, which is how almost every antenna range works.
The Friis equation in decibels is a plain sum, which is why every microwave link is planned as a link budget with a margin.
bank_note: Long answers usually ask you to derive a radiation field from the retarded potential, then use the definitions with numbers, and finish with a link-budget or antenna-choice calculation.

bank.q: Explain the radiation mechanism of an antenna. Why does a charge moving with constant velocity not radiate while an accelerating charge does?
outline: Static charge: field lines closed, no outward flow
Constant velocity: field moves with charge, no kink
Acceleration: kink in field lines detaches and travels as radiation
Two components: 1/r² stored field and 1/r radiated field
Radiated power leaves and never returns to the source

bank.q: Define radiation pattern, directivity, gain and half-power beamwidth. How is gain related to directivity?
outline: Pattern: field or power vs angle, normalised
Main lobe, side lobes, nulls, front-to-back ratio
D = 4πU_max/P_rad, isotropic D = 1
G = e_cd·D, dB conversion
HPBW from the −3 dB points of the main lobe

bank.q: Distinguish radiation resistance, loss resistance and input impedance of an antenna, and define radiation efficiency.
outline: R_r: equivalent resistor for radiated power
R_L: conductor and dielectric loss
Z_in = R_r + R_L + jX_in
e_cd = R_r/(R_r + R_L)
Resonance means X_in ≈ 0, not maximum efficiency

bank.q: Write the Friis transmission equation and explain every symbol. State the assumptions under which it is valid.
outline: P_r = P_t G_t G_r (λ/4πd)²
Symbols: powers in W, gains dimensionless, λ and d in m
Assumptions: far field, free space, polarisation and impedance matched, no multipath
Path loss term (λ/4πd)²
Decibel form Pr = Pt + Gt + Gr − FSPL

bank.q: An infinitesimal dipole of length l = λ/50 carries a current of 2 A at 300 MHz. Find its radiation resistance and the power radiated.
outline: R_r = 80π²(l/λ)² Ω
P_rad = ½I²R_r with I peak, or I_rms²R_r
Answer in mW range
Comment: such a short element is a poor radiator

bank.q: A half-wave dipole radiates 10 W. Find the power density and the electric field strength at 5 km on the broadside direction.
outline: D = 1.64, U_max = D·P_rad/4π
S = P_rad·D/(4πr²)
Numeric substitution r = 5000 m
E = √(2η₀S) with η₀ = 377 Ω
Units: W/m² and V/m

bank.q: A 900 MHz link spans 12 km. Transmitter power is 2 W, both antennas are half-wave dipoles with 2.15 dBi gain. Compute received power in dBm using a link budget.
outline: Convert Pt to dBm: 33 dBm
FSPL = 20log₁₀d(km) + 20log₁₀f(MHz) + 32.44
Add both gains 2.15 + 2.15
Pr = Pt + Gt + Gr − FSPL
Result near −80 dBm, compare with receiver sensitivity

bank.q: Find the far-field distance for a 1.2 m dish at 6 GHz and state which region a 20 m measurement distance lies in.
outline: Answer 57.6 m
20 m is inside the Fresnel (radiating near) region
Pattern measured there will not match the far-field pattern

bank.q: A folded dipole is fed by a 300 Ω twin line. Show numerically why the folded dipole suits this feed better than a simple half-wave dipole.
outline: Half-wave dipole R_in ≈ 73 Ω
Folded dipole R_in ≈ 4 × 73 ≈ 292 Ω
Reflection coefficient |Γ| = |(Z_L − Z₀)/(Z_L + Z₀)|
Compare VSWR and return loss for 292 Ω vs 73 Ω on a 300 Ω line
Conclusion: near-match, wider usable bandwidth

bank.q: Compare the half-wave dipole, quarter-wave monopole and small loop for a 433 MHz low-power sensor. Discuss size, impedance, efficiency and pattern.
outline: Physical size at 433 MHz: λ ≈ 0.69 m
Dipole 73 Ω, D = 2.15 dBi, balanced feed needs a balun
Monopole 36.5 Ω, D = 5.15 dBi, needs a ground plane
Small loop: tiny R_r, loss dominated, needs tuning capacitor
Choose on ground-plane availability, bandwidth and efficiency

bank.q: Derive the far field of a Hertzian dipole from the retarded vector potential and identify the 1/r, 1/r² and 1/r³ terms.
outline: A_z = μ₀Il e^(−jβr)/(4πr)
H = (1/μ₀)∇×A, then E from ∇×H
Result terms in 1/r, 1/r², 1/r³
In far field only 1/r survives; Eθ/Hφ = η₀
Pattern sin θ, no radiation along the axis

bank.q: A receiver needs −95 dBm. With 20 dBm transmit power, 3 dBi at each end and 4 dB of cable and connector loss at each side, find the maximum range at 2.4 GHz and comment on the margin.
outline: EIRP = Pt + Gt − L_tx
Allowed path loss = EIRP + Gr − L_rx − sensitivity
FSPL = 20log d + 20log f + 32.44 solved for d
Compute d in metres or km
Discuss margin for rain, fading and body loss

bank.q: Explain reciprocity and effective aperture. Use them to justify measuring an antenna's gain in transmit mode and then using that gain for reception.
outline: Statement of reciprocity and its consequence for Z, pattern, gain
A_e = λ²D/4π derivation from power density
A_e of a half-wave dipole ≈ 0.13λ², isotropic λ²/4π
Receive power P_r = S·A_e·polarisation loss
Practical range measurement and why one measurement suffices

bank.q: Explain near-field and far-field regions with a labelled sketch, and describe what goes wrong if a pattern is measured in the near field.
outline: Reactive near field r < 0.62√(D³/λ)
Fresnel region up to 2D²/λ
Fraunhofer region beyond, planar wavefront
Reactive energy storage, mutual coupling to probe
Errors: beam broadening, wrong nulls, impedance change

glossary.def: A structure that converts a guided wave on a transmission line into a wave in free space, or the reverse.
A hypothetical antenna radiating equally in all directions; its directivity is exactly 1 (0 dBi).
Power radiated per unit solid angle, U = r²S, measured in W/sr.
Power crossing unit area of a sphere around the antenna, S = E²/(2η₀), in W/m².
The lobe of a pattern containing the direction of maximum radiation.
Any lobe other than the main lobe; it wastes power and causes interference.
The ratio of maximum forward radiation to radiation in the exactly backward direction.
The solid angle through which all the radiated power would flow at peak intensity; Ω_A = 4π/D.
The ratio of a horn or dish's effective area to its physical area, typically 0.5 to 0.7.
−20log₁₀|Γ| in dB, the fraction of incident power reflected back at the antenna terminals.
Voltage standing wave ratio on the feed line, (1+|Γ|)/(1−|Γ|); 1 means a perfect match.
Z_in = R_r + R_L + jX_in, the impedance the feed line sees at the antenna terminals.
The ratio of radiated power to input power, e_cd = R_r/(R_r + R_L).
Ratio of the major to minor axis of the polarisation ellipse; 1 (0 dB) means circular polarisation.
The loss from misalignment between the wave's polarisation and the antenna's, given by |ê_wave · ê_ant|².
The region within about 0.62√(D³/λ) where stored reactive energy dominates.
The radiating near field between the reactive region and 2D²/λ, where the pattern changes with distance.
The far field beyond 2D²/λ, where the wave is locally planar and pattern is distance independent.
A device that connects a balanced antenna such as a dipole to an unbalanced coaxial line.
Replacing an infinite ground plane by a mirror image of the source, used to analyse monopoles over a ground plane.
The spreading loss (4πd/λ)² in the Friis equation, expressed in dB as 20log₁₀d + 20log₁₀f + 32.44 with d in km and f in MHz.
The smallest received power, usually in dBm, at which a receiver still meets its specified error rate.
The extra decibels a link budget keeps above the sensitivity threshold to survive fading and rain.
